doc.title: Houston Person Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 2, 1998 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Technology, CDs and the LP stretching tunes
summary: Person distrusts reliance on technology, adding up ledgers by hand, and says the LP led musicians to stretch tunes rather than add more.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: That’s a great point. And it’s interesting how the technology has allowed other things to happen but perhaps not all that positive. I mean you have — to do a CD now, you’re expected to do almost an hour of music.

Well the way I feel is you know with technology, you know, things don’t necessarily get better. Because a lot of people rely on it too much. And computers still break down. Now you’ve got people who can’t add without a calculator. So I don’t rely on technology. I mean I still like to add. My brother and I we always, when we check the ledger books for our little business in South Carolina, I still add, you know, and subtract, manually.

Yeah, but I enjoy it. I enjoy the thrill of doing those things. But so with music, a lot of people now use music, well it’s really worked against a lot of musicians, starting with the LP. Because instead of adding more tunes they just stretched the ones they were already playing. So I’m trying to add more melodies, more tunes, and still edit and keep the songs at a reasonable length. Now if you get something going and you’ve got it going then say it. But I like that 78 feel, the way you get in there and get out.
